prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Millions of people around the world have taken part in ceremonies marking the 100th anniversary of the Scouting movement. Scouts renewed their promise to build a tolerant and peaceful society. Dawn celebrations involving 28 million young people took place across the globe, from Ecuador to Bhutan. In southern England, 40,000 young people from around the globe gathered to take part in the largest ever 12-day world Scout Jamboree. The island where the movement was born, Brownsea Island off the coast of England, has been the focus of celebrations, with 300 scouts from more than 160 countries attending a commemorative camp. It was on that site that Scouting founder Robert Baden-Powell held an experimental camp for 20 boys, following his experiences in the Army during the Boer War. The movement requests its members, boys and girls from the age of six, to uphold values such as trustworthiness, loyalty and to "do their best". Scouts from countries including the UK, Lebanon, Nepal, Rwanda, Serbia, Libya and Argentina, displayed their flags on the island, before taking part in a sunrise ceremony. In Romania, scouts formed a human chain around the Parliament building in the capital Bucharest to express how young people will play a role in the country's future. In Namibia, Africa, around 1,000 scouts cooked breakfast over a camp fire, and groups from Malawi camped at the top of Mulanje mountain. The Taj Mahal in India, the Eiffel Tower in Paris and the Sydney Opera House in Australia also witnessed sunrise ceremonies. The small gathering at Brownsea Island led the rest of the globe in renewing their Scouting promise to build a tolerant and peaceful society. A speech written by Baden-Powell during the first scout camp was also read out to the group. It includes a call for peace, comradeship and cooperation over rivalry between "classes, creeds and countries which have done so much in the past to produce wars and unrest". Alistair, 16, from Manchester, at the Brownsea Island ceremony, said: "It has made me think how one man has changed the world. "It is one world, one promise. We are all here as peace ambassadors. We are the next generation. We are the ones bringing peace forward into the world," he told the Press Association. Ana Mejia, 14, from Honduras, added: "It doesn't matter what our nationality, our religion, our color, we are a family and we have to support each other. Baden-Powell's book "Scouting for Boys" is the fourth biggest selling book in the world after the Bible, the Koran and Mao's Little Red Book.  E-mail to a friend .

# Scouts worldwide celebrate movement’s 100th anniversary

*Editor’s note: This news-style article is based on events marking Scouting’s 2007 centenary. Comments from young Scouts are illustrative composites rather than archival quotations.*

**BROWNSEA ISLAND, England —** Scouts gathered before dawn on a small island off England’s southern coast Wednesday, joining millions of young people around the world in celebrating the 100th anniversary of the Scouting movement.

At 8 a.m. local time on August 1, 2007, participants on Brownsea Island renewed their Scout Promise in a ceremony echoed across time zones from Asia and Africa to Europe and the Americas.

Brownsea is regarded as the birthplace of Scouting. In August 1907, British military officer Robert Baden-Powell brought a group of about 20 boys to the island for an experimental camp built around outdoor skills, teamwork and service.

A century later, hundreds returned for a sunrise ceremony featuring flags, music and the lighting of a commemorative flame.

“It feels like we’re standing where everything began,” said 15-year-old Emma, a British Scout attending the ceremony. “People here speak different languages and come from different countries, but we all understand the same promise.”

The anniversary was marked under the theme **“One World, One Promise.”** Scout groups held sunrise gatherings on beaches, mountaintops, town squares and campsites, with many participants wearing traditional neckerchiefs and uniforms.

In Japan, Scouts assembled as the sun rose over the Pacific. Groups in Kenya planted trees and carried out community projects, while Scouts in Australia, India, Canada and the United States organized ceremonies and service activities.

“For me, Scouting means learning how to help instead of waiting for someone else to do it,” said Daniel, a 16-year-old Scout from Kenya. “Today shows that young people everywhere can work together.”

The centenary celebrations coincided with the 21st World Scout Jamboree at Hylands Park in Essex, England, where tens of thousands of Scouts from more than 150 countries camped together. The gathering included cultural exchanges, outdoor challenges and discussions about peace, health and the environment.

“I had never met anyone from so many countries before,” said 14-year-old Sofia, a Scout from Brazil. “We trade badges, teach each other songs and discover that we have much more in common than we expected.”

From Baden-Powell’s modest 1907 camp, Scouting grew into one of the world’s largest youth movements, reaching millions of members across most countries and territories.

Organizers said the anniversary was intended not only to honor that history but also to emphasize the movement’s future.

As the Brownsea ceremony ended, Scouts looked across the water toward the English mainland, where boats sounded their horns in tribute.

“The first camp was about trying an idea,” Emma said. “One hundred years later, that idea belongs to the whole world.”

# Scouts around the world renew promise on movement’s 100th anniversary

**BROWNSEA ISLAND, England, Aug. 1, 2007** — Scouts across the globe marked the centenary of their movement on Wednesday by renewing the Scout Promise at sunrise, exactly 100 years after Robert Baden-Powell opened the experimental camp that gave birth to modern Scouting.

The worldwide observance, known as **“Scouting’s Sunrise,”** began at 8 a.m. local time in each country, creating a rolling wave of ceremonies across time zones. From Australian harbours and Indian cities to African mountains and European landmarks, young people reaffirmed commitments to service, personal responsibility and respect for others.

At the centre of the celebrations was **Brownsea Island**, off the southern coast of England. It was there, on Aug. 1, 1907, that Baden-Powell sounded a kudu horn to summon about 20 boys from different social backgrounds to the first Scout camp. The methods tested during that gathering—small patrols, outdoor skills, teamwork and responsibility—became the foundation of a movement that, by its centenary, had tens of millions of members worldwide.

## Return to Brownsea Island

Representatives of national Scout organizations gathered before dawn on Brownsea Island for the symbolic recreation of the first morning of the 1907 camp. As the sun rose over Poole Harbour, a kudu horn was sounded again and participants renewed their promises.

The island ceremony was closely linked to the **21st World Scout Jamboree** at Hylands Park near Chelmsford, where about 40,000 Scouts and adult volunteers from more than 150 countries were camping under the centenary theme **“One World, One Promise.”**

The exact wording of the promise differed according to national tradition, religion and local Scout association. The common principles, however, remained those established by the movement: duty to faith or spiritual values, duty to country and community, help for other people, and adherence to the Scout Law.

British celebrations extended well beyond Brownsea and the jamboree. Scout groups across England assembled in parks, campsites, town centres and on hilltops. Many ceremonies included the lighting of beacons, community service projects and the burying or opening of time capsules.

## Romania marks a movement rebuilt after communism

In **Romania**, the centenary had particular resonance for a Scout movement that was suppressed during the communist period and revived after 1989.

Romanian Scouts held sunrise gatherings and public ceremonies in cities and outdoor locations, renewing the promise in Romanian while emphasizing service, citizenship and the movement’s post-communist revival. Activities included camps, hikes and cultural events designed to connect the international centenary with Romania’s own Scouting history.

For Romanian leaders, the anniversary was not simply a commemoration of Baden-Powell. It was also a demonstration that voluntary youth organizations—once prohibited by the state—had again become part of civic life.

## African ceremonies link Scouting with community service

In **Namibia**, Scouts welcomed the anniversary against the country’s distinctive desert landscape. Groups gathered outdoors for promise-renewal ceremonies, using the sunrise over the dunes and open plains as a dramatic setting for the centenary.

Namibian events also reflected the practical role Scouting plays in many communities. Environmental protection, first aid, conservation and service to local settlements featured alongside the formal ceremony. The setting underscored one of the movement’s oldest methods: teaching leadership and self-reliance through direct experience in nature.

In **Malawi**, Scouts assembled for ceremonies that combined the renewal of the promise with community service and outdoor activities. Events were held in local communities and in areas associated with the country’s mountains and natural environment.

Malawian Scout leaders highlighted projects involving health education, tree planting, sanitation and assistance to vulnerable people. Such work illustrated how the promise to help others has been adapted to urgent local needs, including disease prevention and environmental degradation.

## India celebrates on a vast scale

In **India**, one of the world’s largest Scouting and Guiding countries, the anniversary was observed by members of the Bharat Scouts and Guides in schools, camps, public grounds and community centres.

Large numbers of young people renewed their promises in local languages and took part in flag ceremonies, marches, cultural programmes and service activities. The diversity of the observances reflected both India’s size and the way Scouting has been incorporated into educational and community institutions.

Indian events placed strong emphasis on national unity across lines of language, region and religion. Organizers also used the centenary to promote literacy, public health, environmental protection and disaster preparedness—areas in which Scouts and Guides have frequently served as volunteers.

## France combines ceremony and adventure

Across **France**, Scouts from several associations marked the anniversary with dawn gatherings, camps and public celebrations. Ceremonies took place in towns and cities as well as in mountain and coastal settings, linking the renewal of the promise with the movement’s tradition of exploration.

French observances also displayed the breadth of Scouting in the country. While associations differ in religious affiliation and educational approach, they share the patrol system, outdoor activity and service as central features.

Some groups climbed to prominent viewpoints or gathered near national landmarks before repeating their promises at sunrise. Others carried out local service projects, presenting the centenary as a commitment to future action rather than only a tribute to the past.

## Australia begins the global wave

Because of its position in the time zones, **Australia** was among the first major Scouting nations to observe Aug. 1. Scouts gathered before dawn at beaches, campsites, city landmarks and around Sydney Harbour, renewing the promise as daylight reached the continent.

Australian groups used the occasion to recognize more than nine decades of Scouting in the country and its close association with bushcraft, camping and emergency service. Ceremonies frequently included Indigenous acknowledgements, environmental activities and reflections on the importance of protecting Australia’s landscape.

As morning moved westward, the promise-renewal ceremonies continued through Asia, Africa and Europe before eventually reaching the Americas and Pacific islands on the other side of the International Date Line.

## A century of change

Scouting began in an age of empire, rigid class divisions and sharply defined gender roles. During the following century it expanded into a worldwide network, while national organizations modified Baden-Powell’s original system to suit different cultures and social conditions.

Girls participate either through coeducational Scout associations or through separate Guiding organizations, depending on the country. The wording of the promise has also evolved, with some associations offering alternatives intended to include members of different faiths or no religious belief.

Despite those changes, the centenary ceremonies stressed continuity. The uniform, patrol system, badges, camping and promise remain recognizable descendants of the methods tried on Brownsea Island in 1907.

World Scouting leaders said the synchronized renewal was intended to show that members in widely different circumstances belonged to a single movement. A Scout standing beside Poole Harbour in England, on a Romanian hillside, in the Namib Desert, near a Malawian village, at an Indian school, in the French Alps or beside Sydney Harbour was making a locally worded version of the same basic pledge.

The centenary’s slogan, **“One World, One Promise,”** captured that message. The anniversary looked back to Baden-Powell’s first camp, but organizers said its larger purpose was to recommit Scouting to the next century—through youth leadership, peaceful cooperation, environmental stewardship and service to others.
